catalog_quote: [Hepner 2006:15] Stress is contrastive in Bargam. However there are obvious stress patterns which permit the formation of a general rule with certain basic exceptions. Stress is normally on the ultima if it is closed and on the penultimate syllable if the ultima is not closed. There are two general exceptions to the above rule. The first is that in two- or three-syllable words containing more than one closed syllable the stress is usually drawn to the first closed syllable in the word. This is particularly true of reduplicated forms, which retain the stress pattern of the unreduplicated stem. The second exception involves inalienably possessed nouns, which often retain the stress pattern of the unaffixed stem. This frequently results in antepenultimate stress patterns for these forms. 6) ‘ayin ‘jealousy’ a’yan ‘his cousin’ / a’bitan ‘house of’ abi’tan ‘end’ / ‘danib ‘on the road’ da’nid…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default: stress the final syllable if it is closed (CVC), otherwise the penult; i.e. a right-edge quantity-sensitive pattern where a closed ultima attracts stress. Residual lexical contrast exists (minimal pairs such as 'danib 'on the road' vs da'nid 'comb', a'bitan 'house of' vs abi'tan 'end'), so stress is described as contrastive with low functional load (OPD 1992 p.3 says the same: 'Stress is contrastive in Bargam, but the functional load is not very high. Normally the stress is on the last syllable if it is closed and on the second last if the last syllable is open.').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; contraction discussion (p.17) mentions forms 'manifesting a single primary stress' but no secondary-stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) In 2-3 syllable words with more than one closed syllable, stress usually goes to the first closed syllable; reduplicated forms keep the stress of the unreduplicated stem. (2) Inalienably possessed nouns often keep the stress of the unaffixed stem, frequently yielding antepenultimate stress (e.g. a'lilowan 'feather', a'duman 'core'); dative -ib contraction (p.16-17) deletes the unstressed ultima vowel after a stressed vowel. Clitics are unstressed and take stress from their host (3.16).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation forms (examples are isolated words marked with '). Intonation section (2.3.2, p.15) separately notes commands carry exaggerated stress on the sentence-final syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Bargam (also called Mugil after the mission/plantation ground name; Z'graggen 1971 'Mugil'), ISO mlp = Glottolog barg1252, spoken in the Sumgilbar LLG area, Madang Province; OPD locates data at Gibirin. No dialect restriction stated for the stress description; Hepner 1989 Bargam Dialect Survey is cited for dialect variation generally.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3.1 p.15: stress is contrastive but rule-governed: on the ultima if closed, else penult; exceptions: 2-3 syllable words with more than one closed syllable draw stress to the first closed syllable (esp. reduplications keep stem stress); inalienably possessed nouns keep stem stress, often giving antepenultimate stress. Eight minimal/near-minimal pairs given. Also p.16-17 contraction rule conditioned by preceding stressed vowel; p.15 commands have exaggerated stress on sentence-final syllable; 3.16 clitics take stress from host.
